greekgods|: The Olympian gods each preside over a facet of human life: war, love, craft, trade. They quarrel among themselves and take sides in human affairs, as in Homer's Iliad.
buddhism|Buddhism: A contemplative tradition that studies experience from the inside through meditation, teaching that the self is constructed and that suffering comes from attachment. Its insight practice (vipassanā) aims at seeing directly that everything in experience, the self included, is impermanent.
aristotle|The unmoved mover: Aristotle argued that if anything in the universe changes, something must ultimately drive that change without itself being moved. He called this 'prime mover' a god, but a spare one: it does nothing except think about thinking, and moves the heavens only as an object of desire.
christianity|The Catholic Church: The religion built on the life and teaching of Jesus; from late antiquity to the early modern age the Catholic Church dominated Western civilisation. Beyond its beliefs, it was an organisation: medieval Christendom saw itself as one community under the Church, bound by canon law.
descartes|Mind-body dualism: Descartes divided reality into extended stuff (res extensa) and thinking stuff (res cogitans), which leaves the puzzle of how the two interact. That puzzle set the agenda for later discussion of the mind-body relation.
james|: A groundbreaking textbook by the man often called the father of American psychology, known for its descriptions of the stream of consciousness, attention and the self.
turing|Computing Machinery and Intellige: The paper that asks 'Can machines think?' and replaces the question with an imitation game, later called the Turing test: a machine passes if a judge cannot reliably tell its conversation from a human's. It also answers a list of objections, including one from telepathy.
vonneumann|Babbage, Zuse, von Neumann: Babbage designed a mechanical general-purpose computer in the 1830s; Zuse built the first working programmable computers in Germany around 1941; von Neumann's 1945 report described the stored-program architecture still used today, building on designs by Eckert and Mauchly.
cybernetics|Cybernetics: The mid-century science of control and feedback in animals and machines, born from 1940s exchanges across many disciplines, including early work on neural networks. Norbert Wiener's 1948 book popularised the name; feedback was its central theme, and purposeful behaviour one of its first topics.
physicalism|Physicalism: The thesis that everything that exists is physical or depends on the physical, with no extra mental or supernatural ingredients. It is the majority view among philosophers (about 52% in a 2020 survey), though far from unanimous.
minsky|Perceptrons: A mathematical analysis showing that single-layer neural networks cannot learn certain simple functions. It is often thought to have caused the decline in neural network research in the 1970s and early 1980s, when major funding was hard to find, though how much it was to blame is disputed.
gaia|: The proposal that life on Earth, together with its inorganic surroundings, forms a self-regulating system that keeps the planet's atmosphere and climate suitable for life. James Lovelock and Lynn Margulis proposed it in the 1970s.
sloman|: Philosopher and AI researcher at the University of Birmingham. He argued that philosophy of mind should be done by designing working minds, and he proposed the CogAff scheme that sorts mental processes into reactive, deliberative and reflective layers.
thatcher|The dress: A viral photograph of a dress that some people saw as white and gold and others as blue and black. The cause is not settled; one explanation is that their visual systems made different assumptions about the lighting.
quantumcomp|: Computers that use quantum superposition and entanglement to solve certain problems, such as factoring, far faster than any known classical method. Building them is hard because qubits lose their quantum states (decohere) unless they are well isolated from the environment.
cyc|: A decades-long project to hand-code millions of common-sense facts and rules so that a machine could reason like a person. Doug Lenat started it in 1984; critics such as Pedro Domingos have called it a catastrophic failure.
boltzmannmachine|: A neural network in which units constrain each other and the whole network tends toward low-energy states consistent with the inputs. The restricted version (RBM) drops within-layer links to make training feasible and helped launch deep learning.
occ|: A widely used scheme that sorts emotions into types according to how a person appraises events, agents and objects. Many software agents and artificial characters use it to generate emotions.
ncc|Christof Koch: Neuroscientist who pioneered the search for neural correlates of consciousness with Francis Crick and later helped develop and champion integrated information theory (IIT).
schmidhuber|: The idea that learning is data compression, that curiosity is the reward for finding better compressions, and that beauty is how compressible something already is to the observer.
egan|: Hard science fiction about minds that run as software: copies of people living in simulations, citizens who are programs, and what personal identity means when a mind can be copied.
hypercomputation|: Hypothetical machines that compute more than a Turing machine, for example by using infinitely precise real numbers, or by exploiting special spacetimes in which an endless computation finishes in finite time for an observer.
fields|: Physicist at the Allen Discovery Center at Tufts University who applies quantum information theory to biology and cognition, often with Michael Levin and Karl Friston. He argues that generic physical systems can be regarded as observers exchanging information with their environment.
deeplearning|Stable Diffusion: An openly released image-generation model whose weights fit in about four gigabytes yet can generate photo-realistic images from any text prompt.
marcus|: Cognitive scientist and a well-known critic of deep learning. He argues that neural networks cannot reason reliably without built-in symbolic structure and that scaling them up will not yield general intelligence.
goedel|: Gödel proved that any consistent formal system whose axioms can be listed mechanically and that is rich enough to do arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, and cannot prove its own consistency. He did it by encoding statements about the system as numbers inside the system.
brooks|: Brooks argued that intelligence should be grown from the bottom up in robots that act in the world, using layers of simple behaviours with no central world model. He co-founded iRobot, the company that makes the Roomba.
